He rebuilt Jerusalem's temple on a scale that astonished the ancient world, leveling the mountaintop and doubling the temple platform. He built the harbor at Caesarea, the fortress at Masada, the desert palace of Herodium, and a string of cities around the eastern Mediterranean. His architectural legacy was unmatched in the Levant.

Matthew records his last act in the gospel: hearing of a child born king of the Jews from magi from the east, he ordered the killing of every boy in Bethlehem under two years old. He died, agonized and despised, soon afterward. His kingdom was divided among three surviving sons.

references.note: The magi and the massacre at Bethlehem
In the days of Herod, king of Judea

relationships.description: Sought to kill the child whose magi he had received.
Son who inherited Galilee and Perea.

name: Annas
description: Five sons all became high priests; he was the man behind Caiaphas at Jesus's trial.
biography: Annas held the high priesthood from 6 to 15 AD when the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus deposed him. Five of his sons became high priest in succession, as did his son-in-law Caiaphas; he retained de facto authority over the priestly aristocracy long after his official deposition.

Luke and John both name him alongside Caiaphas as 'the high priest' during the trial of Jesus and the early apostolic preaching — a Hebrew form of authority that did not match the Roman calendar of office. The arresting party brought Jesus to him first, in the small hours of the night.

He questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching; Jesus answered, 'why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me.' A guard struck him for the answer. Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas. He was still alive a generation later, presiding over the court that condemned James, the brother of Jesus, in 62 AD.

references.note: In the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas
Annas the high priest at the trial of Peter and John

relationships.description: Son-in-law and the public face of his continuing authority.
Interrogator before whom Jesus was brought first by night.

name: Herod Antipas
fullName: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea
description: The Herod of Jesus's adult life; the man who beheaded John the Baptist.
biography: Antipas was the second son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan wife Malthace. On his father's death in 4 BC he received Galilee and Perea as tetrarch. He built the city of Tiberias on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee and named it for the emperor.

He married his brother Philip's wife Herodias and was rebuked for it by John the Baptist. Herodias kept her grudge. At a birthday feast her daughter Salome danced; the king swore a public oath to give her up to half his kingdom; she asked, at her mother's bidding, for John's head on a platter. He was beheaded at Machaerus.

Years later, when Pilate learned Jesus was a Galilean, he sent him to Antipas, who was in Jerusalem for Passover. Antipas had long wanted to see Jesus do a sign; Jesus answered him nothing. Antipas mocked him in elegant robes and sent him back. Jesus had once called him 'that fox.' He was eventually banished to Gaul by Caligula and died in exile.

references.note: The beheading of John the Baptist

relationships.description: Father whose kingdom he inherited in part.
The prophet whose rebuke he silenced with a sword.
'That fox' to whom Pilate sent Jesus at the trial.

name: Caiaphas
description: High priest who said it was expedient that one man die for the people.
biography: Caiaphas was appointed high priest by Valerius Gratus around 18 AD and held the office until 36 AD — an unusually long tenure that suggests careful management of his Roman overseers. He was married to Annas's daughter and worked in concert with his father-in-law.

When the Sanhedrin debated what to do about Jesus after Lazarus's raising, Caiaphas said it was expedient that one man die for the people, lest the whole nation perish. John reads the line as an unwitting prophecy: he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only.

He presided over Jesus's nighttime trial, tore his garments at the answer 'I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power,' and pronounced the charge of blasphemy. He sent Jesus bound to Pilate for sentencing. His ossuary, inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas,' was discovered in Jerusalem in 1990.

references.note: Expedient that one man should die
Among the rulers at the trial of Peter and John

relationships.description: Father-in-law and senior partner in the priestly establishment.
The high priest who condemned him for blasphemy.

name: Mary
description: Mother of Jesus, present from his birth to the cross.
biography: A young woman of Nazareth betrothed to Joseph, Mary said yes to the angel Gabriel's announcement and bore Jesus in Bethlehem. Her song — the Magnificat — speaks of a God who topples the proud and lifts up the lowly.

She appears at pivotal moments throughout the Gospels: the flight to Egypt, the wedding at Cana, the foot of the cross, and the upper room at Pentecost — a quiet, steady presence across the whole arc of her son's life and the early days of the church.
Tradition places her later years in Ephesus under the care of John the apostle. She is remembered first as the one who heard the impossible and answered, "let it be to me according to your word."

references.note: At the foot of the cross

relationships.description: Bore him in Bethlehem after Gabriel's announcement.

name: Pontius Pilate
description: Roman prefect who washed his hands and crucified the innocent man before him.
biography: Pilate was appointed prefect of Judea in 26 AD under the emperor Tiberius. His ten-year tenure was marked by harsh confrontations with the Jewish population — bringing imperial standards into Jerusalem, seizing temple funds for an aqueduct, and the slaughter of Galileans whose blood Jesus is asked to comment on in Luke 13.

He presided over Jesus's Roman trial. Three times he declared he found no guilt in him; three times the crowd shouted for crucifixion. He sent Jesus to Antipas; he offered Barabbas as an alternative; he had Jesus scourged; finally he gave the order and washed his hands in front of the people, declaring himself innocent of this blood.

The Roman historian Tacitus would record, a generation later, that 'the founder of the Christian sect, Christ, had been executed in the reign of Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilatus.' That sentence is among the earliest non-Christian references to Jesus. Pilate was recalled to Rome in 36 AD after a massacre of Samaritans on Mount Gerizim. He disappears from the record there.

references.note: I am innocent of this blood
The Galileans whose blood he mingled with their sacrifices

relationships.description: Roman judge who pronounced the sentence of crucifixion.
Worked alongside him in the trial; sent Jesus from court to court.
To whom Pilate sent Jesus mid-trial, and with whom he reconciled.

name: Nicodemus
description: Pharisee who came to Jesus by night and helped bury him in the open of day.
biography: Nicodemus appears three times in John's Gospel. He came to Jesus at night — a Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin who had been struck by the signs. 'How can a man be born when he is old?' he asked. The conversation that followed contains John 3:16. Nicodemus does not say a further word in the scene.

He appears again at a meeting of the council in chapter 7, where the temple police have failed to arrest Jesus. The Pharisees mock the crowd as ignorant of the law; Nicodemus quietly intervenes: does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? They turn on him: are you from Galilee too?

His third appearance is at the cross. He comes with Joseph of Arimathea and brings a hundred Roman pounds of myrrh and aloes — a king's burial, for a crucified man — and wraps Jesus in linen with the spices. The night-visitor of chapter 3 stands beside the tomb in the open of day.

references.note: Does our law judge a man without a hearing?
A hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes

relationships.description: Came to him by night; buried him in the day.
Fellow secret disciple who took down the body with him.

name: Joseph of Arimathea
description: Wealthy council member who asked Pilate for the body of Jesus and gave him his own new tomb.
biography: Joseph was from Arimathea, a town in the Judean hill country. He was a member of the Sanhedrin — Luke notes he was a good and righteous man who had not consented to their decision. John says he was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews.

When the body of Jesus hung dead on the cross late on the day of preparation, Joseph went boldly to Pilate and asked for it — a public association with a man condemned for sedition. Pilate, surprised that Jesus was already dead, confirmed it with the centurion and gave the body to Joseph.

He took it down, wrapped it in fine linen with the spices Nicodemus had brought, and laid it in his own new tomb — hewn in the rock in the garden, where no one had yet been laid. He rolled a great stone to the entrance and went away. Mary Magdalene watched, and noted the place.

references.note: A rich man who was also a disciple
Boldly went to Pilate and asked for the body
A good and righteous man who had not consented

relationships.description: Wealthy secret disciple who buried him in his own tomb.
Fellow secret disciple who helped him bury the body.
The prefect from whom he requested the body.

name: John the Baptist
description: Wilderness prophet who announced the coming of Christ.
biography: Son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth — a relative of Mary — John appeared in the wilderness in camel-hair garments, calling Israel to repentance and baptizing in the Jordan. Crowds streamed out from Jerusalem to hear him.

He recognized Jesus as the one whose coming he had announced and baptized him in the Jordan. "He must increase," John said of his cousin, "but I must decrease" — a deliberate stepping aside as the ministry he had prepared the way for began.

His public denunciation of Herod Antipas's marriage to his brother's wife led to his imprisonment and beheading at the desert fortress of Machaerus. Jesus called him the greatest of those born of women.

relationships.description: Cousin through his mother Elizabeth.
Cousin and the one he baptized in the Jordan.
Came in his spirit and power as the forerunner.

name: Jesus
description: Itinerant Jewish teacher and central figure of the Christian faith.
biography: Born in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great and raised in Nazareth as the son of a craftsman, Jesus lived an obscure life until roughly the age of thirty. He then began a public ministry of teaching, healing, and gathering disciples around him in the towns of Galilee.

His message of the kingdom of God drew crowds and the attention of the religious establishment. He taught in synagogues, on hillsides, and over shared meals — often through parables that subverted the expectations of his hearers.

He was crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate during Passover. His followers proclaimed his resurrection three days later — the foundational claim of the movement that became the Christian church.

relationships.description: Bore him in Bethlehem; stood at his cross.
Cousin and forerunner who baptized him.
Renamed Simon as Peter, 'rock'; restored him after his denial.

name: Andrew
description: First-called of the apostles; the brother who brought Peter to Jesus.
biography: Andrew was a fisherman of Bethsaida, the elder brother of Peter. He had first been a disciple of John the Baptist; when John pointed to Jesus and said 'behold, the Lamb of God,' Andrew followed and spent the day with him. The first thing he did was find his brother: 'we have found the Messiah.' He brought Peter to Jesus.

He appears in three other small moments in the Gospels. At the feeding of the five thousand he is the disciple who notices the boy with the five loaves and two fish. When Greeks came to Jerusalem at Passover wanting to see Jesus, they approached Philip; Philip and Andrew together brought their request to him. On the Mount of Olives he is one of the four who asks Jesus when the end will be.

Beyond the Gospels he disappears from the canonical record. Early tradition has him preaching the gospel in Scythia (modern Ukraine and Russia), Asia Minor, and Greece. He is said to have been crucified at Patras on an X-shaped cross, where the saltire on the flag of Scotland still bears his name.

references.note: Andrew and the boy with five loaves
The Greeks who wished to see Jesus

relationships.description: Older brother whom he brought to Jesus.
Followed him from his first day; brought his brother along.
His first teacher, who pointed him to the Lamb of God.

name: Peter
description: Fisherman, denier, and leader of the apostles; first preacher at Pentecost.
biography: A Galilean fisherman with a brother named Andrew, Simon was renamed Peter — 'rock' — by Jesus at their first meeting. He left his nets at a word and became the first-named of the twelve apostles. He walked on water (briefly), confessed Jesus as the Christ (first), and rebuked him for talking of crucifixion (poorly).

On the night of the arrest he denied three times that he knew the man he had sworn to die with. Days later by the Sea of Galilee, after the resurrection, Jesus asked him three times if he loved him and three times told him to feed the sheep. The denials were undone one by one.

He preached the sermon at Pentecost that began the church and opened it to the Gentiles when he baptized the centurion Cornelius. Tradition holds he was crucified upside down in Rome under Nero, having asked not to die in the same posture as his Lord. Two letters in the New Testament bear his name.

references.note: Do you love me? Feed my sheep

relationships.description: Called him from his nets; renamed him Rock.
Fellow apostle and inner-three companion.
Apostolic colleague; once confronted by Paul at Antioch.
Fellow apostle.
Fellow apostle who fell from the twelve.

name: Judas Iscariot
description: The disciple who betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
biography: One of the twelve, Judas is named in each Gospel list with the addendum that he betrayed Jesus. John notes in passing that he kept the common purse and stole from it. The other Gospels move more quickly to the moment when he went to the chief priests and bargained for thirty pieces of silver — the price, in Exodus, of a slave gored by an ox.

He led the arresting party to Gethsemane and identified Jesus with a kiss. By morning, seeing that Jesus was condemned, he flung the silver back into the temple. The priests would not take it; he hanged himself.

His name has become a byword for betrayal, but the texts that name him do so with surprising restraint. Matthew records his remorse; Acts records the field his blood money bought; the early church preached him neither as a victim of fate nor a simple villain but as a participant in something the Gospel writers could not pretend to fully understand.

relationships.description: Lord and master whom he betrayed for thirty pieces of silver.
Fellow apostle on the road.
Fellow apostle.
Fellow apostle.

name: Zacchaeus
fullName: Zacchaeus, chief tax collector of Jericho
description: Short man who climbed a sycamore to see Jesus and came down a different man.
biography: Zacchaeus was chief tax collector at Jericho — a wealthy and despised man. When the crowd brought Jesus through, he could not see over the heads, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig. Jesus stopped under it. 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.'

He came down at once and welcomed Jesus joyfully. The crowd grumbled — gone in to be the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus stood and announced his repentance in money: half my goods I give to the poor; if I have defrauded anyone, I restore it fourfold. The Mosaic law required fourfold restoration only for sheep-rustlers; he applied it to himself.

Jesus answered with a verdict the crowd had not been ready to hear: 'today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.' Eight verses, one tree, one supper, one man's whole life rearranged.

references.note: Half my goods I give to the poor
The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost

relationships.description: Called him down from the tree by name; ate at his house.

name: Bartimaeus
description: Blind beggar of Jericho who threw off his cloak and was healed.
biography: Bartimaeus sat beside the Jericho road begging. Jesus was coming out of the city with a large crowd. The blind man heard it was Jesus of Nazareth and began to shout, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' The crowd told him to be quiet; he shouted all the louder.

Jesus stopped and said, 'call him.' Bartimaeus threw off his cloak — his only possession, the bowl he begged into — and sprang to his feet. 'What do you want me to do for you?' Jesus asked. 'Rabbouni,' he said, using the most intimate term, 'let me see again.'

Mark preserves his name where the parallel accounts in Matthew and Luke leave the beggar anonymous — perhaps because he became known in the early church. 'Go,' Jesus said, 'your faith has made you well.' And immediately he received his sight and followed him on the way.

relationships.description: Healed his blindness and was followed by him on the way.

name: The Rich Young Ruler
description: Wealthy man who came to Jesus asking what he must do — and went away sorrowful.
biography: Three Gospels preserve the encounter. Matthew calls him young; Luke calls him a ruler; Mark says he ran up, knelt before Jesus, and asked, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' Jesus first deflected the title — why do you call me good? — and listed the commandments.

The young man answered that he had kept them all from his youth. Jesus, looking at him, loved him. 'One thing you lack: go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' His countenance fell. He went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.

The disciples were astonished — surely the wealthy were the visibly blessed. 'How hard it is,' Jesus said, 'for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God.' He never names him. The man stands in scripture as a quiet anonymous failure — the only person recorded as walking sadly away from a direct invitation of Jesus.

references.note: Jesus, looking at him, loved him

relationships.description: Invited him to follow; he walked away sorrowful.

name: Cornelius
fullName: Cornelius, centurion of the Italian Cohort
description: Roman centurion of Caesarea; first Gentile baptized into the church.
biography: Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian Cohort stationed at Caesarea — a Roman officer, a God-fearer who prayed continually and gave alms generously to the Jewish poor. About the ninth hour of the day an angel of God came to him in a vision and told him to send for a man called Peter at Joppa.

Peter meanwhile was on a rooftop in Joppa where a sheet came down from heaven full of unclean animals, with a voice telling him to kill and eat. While he was still puzzling, the messengers from Cornelius arrived. Peter went with them and entered the house of a Gentile — a thing no devout Jew did.

He preached the gospel; the Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius and his household while he was still speaking; the believers from the circumcision were amazed. Peter ordered them baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. The door to the Gentile world had been pushed open with him on the inside.

references.note: Peter's sermon and the Spirit falling on Gentiles
Peter defends the conversion to the Jerusalem church

relationships.description: Apostle who came to his house and opened the gospel to the Gentiles.

name: Lydia
fullName: Lydia of Thyatira, seller of purple
description: First convert on European soil; hosted Paul's mission at Philippi.
biography: Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira in Asia Minor — Thyatira was famed for its dyers' guild — now resident in the Roman colony of Philippi. She was a worshiper of God who gathered with other women at a place of prayer by the river outside the city on the Sabbath.

Paul and his companions had come to Philippi from Troas after Paul's vision of the man of Macedonia. They sat down by the river and spoke to the women there. 'The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.' She and her household were baptized — the first recorded conversion on European soil.

She insisted that Paul and his company stay at her house. She does not appear again in Acts, but Paul's letter to the Philippians remembers the church 'from the first day until now' as his partners in the gospel, with money sent more than once. Lydia's open door at Philippi is the foundation of that partnership.

references.note: Paul and Silas back at her house after prison

relationships.description: Apostle whose preaching by the river opened her heart.
Sat at her river meeting and stayed in her house.

name: Aquila
description: Jewish tentmaker exiled from Rome; companion of Paul and teacher of Apollos.
biography: Aquila was a Jew from Pontus living in Rome when the emperor Claudius issued his edict in 49 AD expelling the Jews from the city. He and his wife Priscilla moved to Corinth and set up their tentmaking business there. Paul, recently arrived from Athens, was a tentmaker too. He stayed and worked with them.

When Paul left Corinth he took them along to Ephesus and left them there. While he was away they heard a brilliant but partial Alexandrian preacher named Apollos in the synagogue; they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

Paul mentions them in three letters as 'fellow workers in Christ Jesus who risked their necks for my life.' By the time he writes Romans they are back in Rome, with a church meeting in their house. By the second letter to Timothy they are in Ephesus again. They had no fixed address but a long, faithful partnership in the spreading mission.

references.note: Together with Priscilla they taught Apollos
Greetings to them and the church in their house

relationships.description: Partner in tentmaking and ministry across three cities.
Apostle who lived and worked with them in Corinth.

name: Stephen
description: First of seven deacons; first Christian martyr; stoned outside Jerusalem.
biography: Stephen was the first of seven Hellenistic Jewish believers chosen to oversee the daily distribution to widows when complaints arose that the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked. Acts calls him 'a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit,' 'full of grace and power,' who did great wonders and signs among the people.

His enemies in the synagogue of the Freedmen could not stand against his wisdom. They suborned false witnesses and brought him before the Sanhedrin. His defense — Acts 7 — is the longest single speech in the book, a sweeping retelling of Israel's history that ends with the accusation that they had killed the prophets and now the Righteous One.

Outraged, the council ground their teeth at him. He looked up and saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. They cast him out of the city and stoned him. A young man named Saul stood watching, holding the coats. As Stephen died he prayed, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.'

references.note: Chosen as one of the seven

relationships.description: Saul of Tarsus held the cloaks at his stoning — and was later haunted by it.
Saw him standing at the right hand of God as he died.

name: Philip the Evangelist
description: One of the seven; evangelist to Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch on the Gaza road.
biography: Philip was the second of the seven deacons appointed in Acts 6 — not to be confused with Philip the apostle. After Stephen's stoning and the scattering of the Jerusalem church, he went down to Samaria and preached the Christ there. Crowds heard him; many believed; demons came out; the city had great joy.

An angel of the Lord sent him next to the south road from Jerusalem to Gaza. He found an Ethiopian official, the treasurer of Candace queen of Ethiopia, riding home in a chariot reading Isaiah 53. Philip ran up; the eunuch invited him into the chariot; Philip began at that very scripture and told him the good news of Jesus. The eunuch saw water and asked to be baptized.

The Spirit carried Philip away; he was found at Azotus and continued preaching through the coastal towns up to Caesarea, where he settled. Twenty years later he hosted Paul on the way to Jerusalem. He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. The first Christian missionary to step decisively outside Judean borders.

references.note: Host to Paul at Caesarea; four daughters who prophesied

relationships.description: Hosted him in Caesarea on the way to Jerusalem.
Fellow deacon of the seven.

name: Felix
fullName: Marcus Antonius Felix, Roman procurator of Judea
description: Procurator before whom Paul defended himself; left him in prison for two years.
biography: Felix was a freedman who rose unusually high under emperors Claudius and Nero, becoming procurator of Judea around 52 AD. Tacitus says he 'practiced every kind of cruelty and lust, wielding the power of a king with the mind of a slave.' He married a series of royal women, ending with Drusilla, sister of Agrippa II.

When Paul was sent to him under armed escort from Jerusalem after the riot in the temple, Felix heard the charges and adjourned to await the testimony of the tribune Lysias — which never came. Paul lingered in custody at Caesarea. Felix sent for him repeatedly and 'reasoned with him about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment.' Felix was alarmed and dismissed him each time, saying, 'when I have an opportunity I will send for you.'

He kept Paul two years, hoping for a bribe. When he was recalled to Rome in 60 AD, he left Paul in prison as a final favor to the Jews. His successor Festus took up the case. Felix had used a Roman court like a slow extortion racket; the prisoner he had hoped to monetize wrote letters in his chains that the empire never managed to silence.

references.note: Felix reasoned with him; hoped for a bribe
Left Paul in prison two years

relationships.description: Roman judge who kept him in chains at Caesarea for two years.

name: Mary Magdalene
description: First witness of the resurrection; called the apostle to the apostles.
birthplace: Magdala, on the Sea of Galilee
biography: Luke introduces her as a woman from whom Jesus had cast out seven demons. From that point she belongs to the small company of women who traveled with him, supported the mission from their own resources, and stayed close where most of the male disciples fell away.

She was at the cross when most of the apostles had fled. She watched where Joseph of Arimathea laid the body. On the third morning she came back with spices to anoint it and found the tomb open and empty — and a gardener standing nearby who said her name.

She was the first to see the risen Christ and the first sent to tell the others. The early church would call her apostola apostolorum: the apostle to the apostles. Centuries of confused legend later identified her with other women in the Gospels; the texts themselves leave her as she is — a Galilean disciple at the center of the Easter narrative.

references.note: Among the women who supported the ministry
At the foot of the cross
Mary, the empty tomb, and the risen Christ

relationships.description: Healed her of seven demons; she became first witness of his resurrection.
Stood with the mother of Jesus at the foot of the cross.
Together at the cross; brought him word of the empty tomb.
Brought him word of the empty tomb on resurrection morning.

name: Martha
description: Sister of Lazarus and Mary; host to Jesus and a confessor of his messiahship.
biography: Martha is introduced as the practical sister: while Mary sat at Jesus's feet listening, Martha was anxious about preparations and asked him to send her sister to help. He gently refused — 'Mary has chosen the good portion' — and Martha is sometimes remembered, unfairly, only for that scene.

When their brother Lazarus fell ill and died, it was Martha who ran out to meet Jesus on the road before he reached the house. Their exchange contains one of the great confessions of the Gospels: he told her that he was the resurrection and the life and asked if she believed it. 'Yes, Lord,' she answered. 'I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.'

She appears once more, hosting Jesus at supper days before his death — still serving, but with the unmistakable warmth of one whose house was always open to him. Her name has come down the centuries as a byword for hospitality and for sturdy, articulate faith.

references.note: Martha and Mary in the home
The death and raising of Lazarus

relationships.description: Older brother whose death she mourned in Bethany.
Welcomed him to her table in Bethany.

name: Lazarus
description: Brother of Martha and Mary; raised from the dead four days after dying.
biography: Lazarus is given few words of his own in scripture; almost everything we know about him is told through the people around him. He, his sister Martha, and his sister Mary lived in Bethany, a village a short walk from Jerusalem, and Jesus loved them all.

When he fell ill, the sisters sent word; Jesus deliberately delayed two days. By the time he arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days — long enough in the warm climate, Martha worried, for the body to stink. Jesus wept at the tomb anyway. Then he called out one name: 'Lazarus, come out.' And Lazarus walked out, still wrapped in his grave clothes.

His public resurrection turned the religious authorities decisively against Jesus; John reports that they also plotted to kill Lazarus, since people were leaving them to follow him. He appears one last time at the supper in Bethany, quietly at table with the man who had called him out of the grave.

references.note: At table with Jesus in Bethany
A separate Lazarus in Jesus's parable

relationships.description: Sister of the household in Bethany.
Called out of the tomb after four days.

name: Paul
description: Apostle to the Gentiles and author of much of the New Testament.
biography: A Pharisee trained in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, Saul of Tarsus first appears in scripture approving the stoning of Stephen and persecuting the early church. A blinding encounter with the risen Christ on the road to Damascus reordered his life entirely.

As Paul, he became the great missionary of the early movement, planting churches across the Roman world on three long journeys and writing the letters that would become foundational scripture for the church.
He was arrested in Jerusalem, appealed his case to Caesar, and was taken under guard to Rome. Tradition holds he was martyred there under the emperor Nero.

relationships.description: Appeared to him on the road to Damascus and called him as apostle.
Fellow apostle; clashed with him at Antioch over Gentile inclusion.
Among the pillars of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2).
Argued that all who have faith are children of Abraham.

name: Thomas
description: The apostle remembered for honest doubt and a definitive confession.
biography: Thomas is named in all four Gospel lists of the apostles, with the Greek nickname Didymus — 'twin.' John's Gospel gives him a voice the others do not. When Jesus turned back toward Bethany after Lazarus's death and danger, it was Thomas who said, 'let us go too, that we may die with him.'

After the resurrection he was missing when Jesus first appeared to the disciples behind locked doors. He told the others he would not believe it until he had seen and touched the wounds himself. A week later Jesus appeared again and offered him exactly that. Thomas answered with what is perhaps the most complete confession of any disciple in the Gospels: 'My Lord and my God.'

Early Christian tradition has him preaching the gospel as far east as India, where the ancient Mar Thoma church still claims him as founder. He is remembered now for a single hesitation, but the words that followed it have echoed through the worship of the church for two thousand years.

references.note: Let us go too, that we may die with him
How can we know the way?

relationships.description: The risen Lord who let him touch the wounds.
Fellow apostle.
Fellow apostle.
Fellow apostle who fell from the twelve.

name: John the Apostle
description: Fisherman, evangelist, and the disciple whom Jesus loved.
biography: John and his brother James — sons of Zebedee, called by Jesus the 'sons of thunder' — were fishermen on the Sea of Galilee when they were summoned to follow. He became one of the inner three with Peter and James, present at the Transfiguration and in Gethsemane, and the only male disciple at the foot of the cross.

Jesus entrusted his mother to him from the cross: 'behold your mother.' He ran with Peter to the empty tomb on the resurrection morning and stooped down to look in. After Pentecost he ministered in Jerusalem and Samaria; tradition places his later years in Ephesus, caring for the church there and for Mary.

Of the twelve, he alone is said to have died of old age — exiled, before that, to the rocky island of Patmos under the emperor Domitian, where he received the visions recorded in Revelation. His Gospel and three letters speak again and again of a single theme: God is love, and we are loved.

references.note: I, John, was on the island called Patmos

relationships.description: The beloved disciple; entrusted with his mother from the cross.
Took her into his care after the cross.
Inner-three companion; ran with him to the empty tomb.
Fellow apostle.
With her at the cross; ran to the tomb at her word.
Pillar of the Jerusalem church alongside Paul (Galatians 2).

name: Priscilla
description: Tentmaker and teacher whose name is often listed before her husband's.
biography: Priscilla (also called Prisca) was the wife of Aquila and his partner in a tentmaking and teaching ministry that spanned three of the most important cities of the early empire. Four of the six New Testament references to the couple list her first — unusual in the ancient world and suggesting she was the more prominent of the two in the Christian community.

She and Aquila met Paul in Corinth, traveled with him to Ephesus, and stayed there as the residual core of the church. When the brilliant but partially-instructed Alexandrian preacher Apollos came through, it was Priscilla and Aquila together who took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately. They were teachers of teachers.

Paul greets them in Romans as 'fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life.' Wherever they moved a church met in their house. They are the only married couple named together with this kind of partnership in the New Testament — a model of shared ministry that the church has never quite known what to do with.

references.note: Risked their necks for my life

relationships.description: Partner in tentmaking and ministry across Rome, Corinth, and Ephesus.
Co-worker who hosted him and traveled with him.

name: Barnabas
description: Son of Encouragement; the man who brought Saul to the apostles and Paul into the Gentile mission.
biography: Joseph the Levite of Cyprus was nicknamed by the apostles Barnabas — Son of Encouragement. His first appearance in Acts is the sale of a field and the laying of the money at the apostles' feet. He next appears bringing the freshly converted Saul to the apostles when they were afraid of him, vouching for him as a true disciple.

When the gospel reached the Gentiles in Antioch and the Jerusalem church needed someone to investigate, they sent Barnabas. He saw the grace of God and was glad. He went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him back to Antioch; for a year they taught the church there. The first missionary journey was theirs together — to Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe.

Their partnership broke at the start of the second journey over John Mark, Barnabas's cousin, whom Paul refused to bring back after he had abandoned the first journey. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus; Paul took Silas and went through Syria and Cilicia. The two great encouragers of the early mission parted ways. Years later Paul refers warmly to both Barnabas and Mark in his letters.

references.note: The break with Paul over John Mark

relationships.description: Co-worker who first vouched for him and partnered the first mission.
Stood with him in the Jerusalem Council.

name: Silas
fullName: Silas (Silvanus), leader of the Jerusalem church
description: Paul's companion on the second journey; sang hymns at midnight in a Philippian jail.
biography: Silas (called Silvanus in the letters) was a leading man among the brethren of Jerusalem and a prophet. He was sent with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch with the council's letter on Gentile inclusion. When Paul and Barnabas split, Paul chose Silas as his partner for the second journey.

At Philippi they cast a demon out of a fortune-telling slave girl, were stripped, flogged, and thrown in the inner cell with their feet in stocks. At midnight they prayed and sang hymns to God; the prisoners listened; an earthquake shook the doors open. The jailer drew his sword to kill himself; Paul called out, 'do yourself no harm, we are all here'; he washed their wounds and was baptized that night with his household.

Silas continued with Paul through Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, and Corinth. He is co-author of both letters to the Thessalonians and probably amanuensis for 1 Peter ('by Silvanus, a faithful brother'). His ministry stretches across two of the great apostolic correspondences.

references.note: Chosen leading man of the church
Singing hymns at midnight in Philippi

relationships.description: Co-author of two letters and partner on the second journey.
Joined them at Lystra and traveled together.
Stayed at her house in Philippi after release from prison.

name: Festus
fullName: Porcius Festus, Roman procurator of Judea
description: Succeeded Felix; heard Paul's appeal to Caesar and sent him to Rome.
biography: Festus took over from Felix in 60 AD and inherited Paul still in custody at Caesarea. Within three days of his arrival he was in Jerusalem, where the chief priests demanded he transfer Paul there for a hearing — they were planning an ambush on the road. Festus refused and called for the accusers to come to Caesarea.

At the hearing he asked Paul whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem to be tried before him. Paul answered, 'I appeal to Caesar.' By Roman law Festus had to refer the case to the emperor. He was relieved — the charges were religious matters incomprehensible to him — but he had no clear crime to put in the letter of transmittal.

He brought Paul before Agrippa II and Bernice during their state visit to Caesarea, asking for help framing the indictment. During Paul's defense Festus shouted out, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you insane!' Paul answered calmly. Festus shipped him to Rome in the autumn of 60 or 61 AD. He died in office in Judea two years later.

references.note: Festus presents the case to Agrippa
Your great learning is driving you insane

relationships.description: Roman judge who shipped him to Rome on his appeal to Caesar.
King to whom he handed Paul for a second hearing.

name: Agrippa
fullName: Herod Agrippa II, king of Chalcis and tetrarch
description: Last of the Herodian dynasty in power; heard Paul's defense and said he was almost persuaded.
biography: Agrippa II was the great-grandson of Herod the Great, raised in the imperial court in Rome. He was given the small kingdom of Chalcis on his uncle's death and later granted northern territories of his great-uncle Philip's old tetrarchy. The Romans gave him oversight of the Jerusalem temple and the right to appoint the high priest.

He was the brother of Drusilla (Felix's wife) and of Bernice, with whom Roman gossip alleged an unsavory closeness. He came to Caesarea on a state visit to greet the new procurator Festus and was invited to hear Paul.

Paul's defense before him traces Paul's life from his Pharisee youth to the road to Damascus and the open invitation of the gospel. He spoke directly to the king: 'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' Agrippa famously replied, 'in a short time you will persuade me to be a Christian.' He died around the end of the first century — the last Herodian ruler, witnessing the fall of his people's capital in 70 AD.

references.note: In a short time you will persuade me to be a Christian

relationships.description: King before whom he gave his most personal defense.
Procurator who invited him to hear Paul.
Great-grandfather and founder of the dynasty he closed.

name: Timothy
description: Paul's true child in the faith; pastor of Ephesus; recipient of two pastoral letters.
biography: Timothy was the son of a Jewish believer named Eunice and a Greek father, raised by his mother and grandmother Lois on the scriptures from childhood. He grew up in Lystra and was already well spoken of by the brothers there when Paul came through on the second journey.

Paul circumcised him to ease his acceptance in the synagogues they were entering — a controversial decision given Titus had not been circumcised. Timothy joined Paul and Silas and became Paul's closest associate for the rest of Paul's life. Six of Paul's letters are co-authored or co-signed by Timothy. Paul sent him on hard missions to Macedonia and Corinth where his own presence was not feasible.

Paul's two letters to him — 1 and 2 Timothy — are the most personal Pauline letters preserved. By the time of 2 Timothy, Paul is in prison facing death and asking Timothy to come quickly. He calls him 'my true child in the faith,' 'my beloved child,' and the heir of his ministry. Tradition has Timothy serving as the first bishop of Ephesus and martyred there in old age.

references.note: Your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice
I have no one like him

relationships.description: Apostle who called him his true child in the faith.
Joined the second journey together at Lystra.

name: Titus
description: Greek convert; Paul's troubleshooter in Corinth and organizer of the church in Crete.
biography: Titus was a Greek and was not circumcised — and Paul refused to circumcise him when they went up to the Jerusalem Council, making him the test case for the inclusion of Gentile believers without the law. The decision in Acts 15 was largely shaped by his uncircumcised presence in the room.

He served Paul as troubleshooter to a series of difficult situations. He carried the painful letter to Corinth and brought back the news of their repentance. He oversaw the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem from the Greek churches. Paul calls him 'my partner and fellow worker for your benefit.'

Paul left him in Crete to set the churches in order and appoint elders in every town. The Letter to Titus is Paul's manual for that work — sober, sound, and lit with one of the great compact summaries of grace in the New Testament: 'the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.' By 2 Timothy he is in Dalmatia.

references.note: Even Titus was not compelled to be circumcised
I left you in Crete that you might put what remained into order

relationships.description: Apostle who sent him as troubleshooter to the hardest churches.
